title: Sign it off for me?
topic: Probity in training, research, audit and applications
stem:
You are an F2 doctor. Your friend Dr Ellis, another F2, has a deadline for her portfolio tonight. She asks you to sign off a supervised learning event for a procedure, saying, "I did it last week, you just weren't there."

You didn't observe the procedure.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Sign it, as she is competent and you trust her.
options.detailed: Even if she is competent, signing without observing is dishonest.

options.text: Decline to sign off something you didn't observe.
options.detailed: A supervised learning event confirms that you observed the procedure. Signing it without seeing it would be a false record.

options.text: Sign it, but write a brief comment so it isn't too detailed.
options.detailed: Keeping the comment brief doesn't change the fact that you didn't observe it.

options.text: Report her to her educational supervisor.
options.brief: Disproportionate for a request you've declined.
options.detailed: She asked, and you can decline. A report at this stage is excessive.

options.text: Tell other colleagues what she asked you to do.
options.detailed: This doesn't help anyone and may damage her standing.

options.text: Suggest she backdates a new assessment with another colleague.
Suggest she asks the person who did observe her.
options.brief: The right person can sign it honestly.
options.detailed: If someone supervised her, they can complete the assessment honestly.

options.text: Offer to observe her doing the procedure soon.
options.detailed: Observing her yourself lets you sign it off honestly, even if it is after the deadline.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you keep training records honest when a friend asks you to help them out.
explanation.keyDetails: You didn't observe the procedure. She is under deadline pressure. She is a friend.
explanation.reasoning: [B] declines honestly, [G] points to the right person, and [H] offers genuine help. The distractors falsify ([A], [C], [F]), overreact ([D]), or gossip ([E]).
explanation.competing: [D] feels principled, but she asked and you declined, so there is nothing to report at this stage.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 4, honesty in training records and assessments.
